h: Hull's free museums and waterfront gems
p: Here's a tip that keeps the costs down: many of Hull's best museums have traditionally been free to visit, and lots of them are within easy walking distance of Princes Quay. In the Old Town, Wilberforce House is the birthplace of William Wilberforce, who campaigned against the slave trade, and it tells that powerful story brilliantly.

Next door, the Streetlife Museum is a big favourite with families, with old buses, trams, carriages and recreated streets to wander through. The Hull and East Riding Museum, in the same museum quarter, has Roman mosaics and a life-size woolly mammoth. Over on Queen Victoria Square, the Ferens Art Gallery has a fantastic collection and hosts big exhibitions.

Hull Minster, the city's huge parish church, is also in the Old Town and well worth a look inside. The cobbled lanes around it are full of historic pubs, some of them tucked down alleys you'd walk straight past if you didn't know they were there.

Down at the marina, the Spurn Lightship is a reminder of the city's long relationship with the sea, and the Fruit Market area by the waterfront has become a lively spot for independent bars, galleries and places to eat.
Hull was UK City of Culture in 2017, and that buzz hasn't completely gone away. Look out for public art, events and festivals across the city during your visit, especially in summer.

Shopping centres like Princes Quay work best as part of a bigger day. Start with a few hours of browsing, grab lunch, then step outside and let the rest of Hull do the hard work. If you're arriving by train, the Paragon Interchange is close by, and it's a straightforward walk past Queens Gardens towards the Old Town. With so much to see in such a small area, it's very easy to pack a lot into one day without needing to drive anywhere.
